items.title: Warhol’s Watches
items.summary:
Piaget’s second collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts translates the pop artist’s 1986 Camouflage self-portraits into dials made of gemstone marquetry. 

Related Articles

What Is Internet Cinema? 

Christie's Adds UK Auction House Dreweatts to Its Portfolio 

Long before luxury watches were as sought after as they are today, Andy Warhol coveted and collected them. Over the course of the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s, the Pop Art pioneer amassed more than 300 timepieces that reflected his high-low tastes. He collected watches the way he collected everything, with an appetite that blurred connoisseurship and compulsion. When Sotheby’s sold his estate in 1988, the sale featured timepieces by Cartier, Bulgari, and Patek Philippe alongside cookie jars and Art Deco furniture. Warhol is often said to have worn watches less to tell time than to be seen in them. For an artist who made a career of elevating the ordinary, a watch was a portable piece of pop culture, a status symbol he could wear and treasure.

Photo Courtesy of Piaget 

One brand, however, stood out. Warhol owned at least seven wristwatches by the Swiss maison, Piaget. Founded in 1874 in La Côte-aux-Fées, a village in the heart of Switzerland’s Jura mountain range, the house was renowned in the latter half of the 20th century for its creative selection of timepieces in unusual shapes, many featuring dials made of exotic ornamental stones. One of those watches, a quartz-powered reference 15102 model that Warhol purchased from the brand in 1973, now forms the foundation for a Piaget collection…
items.t: Warhol’s Watches

items.title: What Is Internet Cinema?
items.summary:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot , a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet. 

During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020.

Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ I am going to die (this is my sign) (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.

A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents…
items.t: What Is Internet Cinema?

items.title: Five Questions for Advisors on the November Marquee Sales: Guarantees, Spotty Bidding, and a $190 M. Van Gogh
items.summary:
Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance , the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday. 

It’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-important November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach. But before we turn to Miami, a quick post-mortem on the marquee sales just passed.

Perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder. Do you measure it by overall totals? By sell-through rate? By the number of bidders, or the number of guaranteed lots? By the ratio of hammer prices to estimates? Each figure tells a slightly different story, leaving plenty for our resident market whisperers to debate. But before we turn this week’s column over to the advisers, let’s set out some basic figures.

According to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022. Sotheby’s led the pack with $1.16 billion, clearing $1 billion and taking more than half of the three houses’ combined total for the second straight year. (Its share rose to 57 percent from 53 percent. Christie’s share dropped to 38 percent from 43 percent, while Phillips’s ticked up to 5 percent from 4 percent, pushed by the $44.6 million Modigliani sculpture. )

And yes, the $384 million gap between Sotheby’s and Christie’s is roughly what the…

items.title: Christie’s Adds UK Auction House Dreweatts to Its Portfolio
items.summary:
Christie’s has added the UK auction house Dreweatts to its portfolio.

In a statement on Wednesday, Christie’s chief executive Bonnie Brennan said that the auction house has long admired Dreweatts. “Most importantly, our clients collect across categories and at every price point, and together we have the opportunity to provide them with an even broader and more complete level of service. Both businesses will continue to operate much as they do today, while building on their respective strengths and the significant opportunities we see for future growth,” she said.

Dreweatts specializes in single-owner collections and country house sales, ranging from furniture and works of art, old masters, modern and contemporary art, Asian and European ceramics, modern design, jewelry, silver, luxury accessories, clocks and wine. The auction house was founded in 1759 by Thomas Davis, a cabinetmaker, upholsterer and land agent from Abingdon, Oxfordshire. Dreweatts operates its main salesroom from its country house, Donnington Priory, in Newbury, Berkshire, and also has a showroom in London on Pall Mall.

Henry House, chief executive of Dreweatts, said in a statement that under this new arrangement “we can use the additional advantage of one another’s expertise to better serve our buyers and sellers. Dreweatts has had a parent company before, which enabled us to grow the business and prosper, and this move is an extension of that model.” He added that the Christie’s acquisition provides certainty for the auction house and that Dreweatts will continue, under his and chairman Will Richards’…
items.t: Christie’s Adds UK Auction House Dreweatts to Its Portfolio

items.title: Former Sotheby’s Vice President Michael Bouhanna Launches Miami-Based Art Advisory
items.summary:
Michael Bouhanna, the former vice president of contemporary art specialist and head of digital art at Sotheby’s, has launched his own art advisory. Called Bouhanna Art Advisory, it will focus on modern and contemporary art based out of Miami.

Bouhanna was the last man standing at Sotheby’s Metaverse and other NFT divisions when the auction house laid off four staffers in 2024. He joined the company in 2016 as CTP junior cataloger and quickly moved up the ranks in the contemporary art department before being given the joint responsibility of contemporary and digital art in 2021. Bouhanna exited Sotheby’s in January, after just over a decade at the auction house working in its London, Paris, and New York headquarters. Bouhanna’s exit was unrelated to the layoffs, although following his departure Sotheby’s integrated NFTs and digital art into its contemporary art department. In September 2025, Christie’s closed its digital art department as the demand for digital art cooled down. In a wider view of the digital art market, Bouhanna told ARTnews that digital art is still part of contemporary art and it should not be seen as a separate entity. “Digital art still interests collectors who follow technology and AI. The serious digital artists have continued to gain institutional recognition, but it’s a niche within contemporary art.”

Bouhanna’s new chapter in Miami will involve placing modern and contemporary art by blue-chip artists in private collections and hands. In Miami, he has started working with private collectors, family offices and estates across acquisitions, sales,…
items.t: Former Sotheby’s Vice President Michael Bouhanna Launches Miami-Based Art Advisory

items.title: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang
items.summary:
SEC Armadillo, Glasgow
The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity

Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist.

The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing, and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life.

Touring Europe until 2 May
items.t: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang

items.title: Venice Biennale Awards Selected by Public Vote Go to Nick Cave, Indian Pavilion
items.summary:
After a Venice Biennale of bitter controversy, the exhibition has at last revealed the winners of its top honors, which were chosen this year by public vote instead of a jury of esteemed curators because that panel resigned in protest. This time around, the awards went to the American artist Nick Cave for his participation in Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition and India for its national pavilion.

Dubbed the Visitors’ Lions, these awards replaced the Golden Lions, which are regularly given to participants in the main exhibition and artists representing countries with pavilions in the exhibition. This time around, just two awards were given out, one for an artist in the main show and one for a national pavilion.

The Biennale was forced to instate the Visitors’ Lions after the five-person Golden Lion jury resigned in May, in advance of the show’s opening. By that point, the curators had already said that they would “refrain from considering those countries whose leaders are currently charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court,” a move that would exclude Israel and Russia from consideration. More than half of the artists in the main show said they would not accept the Visitors’ Lions in solidarity.

Cave’s contributions to the Kouoh’s show, titled “In Minor Keys,” included a decidedly major work: Amalgam ( Origin ), a 26-foot-tall bronze sculpture in which a person’s body sprouts branches and wildlife. The work, which appeared outdoors at the Arsenale, derived from a similar-looking proposal for a piece to replace a toppled Confederate monument.…

items.title: Thelma Golden To Step Down From Role as Director of Studio Museum in Harlem
items.summary:
Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her position in late 2027, the museum announced Tuesday.

The announcement coincides with Golden’s 20th anniversary in the role, which she assumed in 2006, and comes just one year after the museum reopened in a new, purpose-built building after a seven-year closure. The new $125 million building was designed by architect David Adjaye and provides 82,000 square feet across seven floors, including a 139-seat public lobby, a rooftop terrace, education spaces, a library, and a cafe. It received rave reviews upon its reopening.

Kathryn C. Chenault, chair of the museum’s board of trustees, said in a statement that the board has formed a search committee to identify Golden’s successor and has retained an international executive search firm to assist. Golden will remain in her post until a replacement is hired.

While Golden’s departure was not entirely expected, it is not unusual for museum directors to exit their positions after a major renovation or expansion. Lisa Phillips announced in September 2025 that she would leave her role as director of the New Museum after its reopening, and Janne Sirén, director of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, said in April that he would step down following the museum’s 2023 expansion.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to new projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors,…
items.t: Thelma Golden To Step Down From Role as Director of Studio Museum in Harlem

items.title: Military History Museum in Dresden Agrees to Return Contested Nazi-Era Family Archive to Jehovah’s Witnesses
items.summary:
Five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the New York Times . Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history published by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau.

At the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official…
items.t: Military History Museum in Dresden Agrees to Return Contested Nazi-Era Family Archive to Jehovah’s Witnesses

items.title: Bukhara Biennial Unveils ‘The Long Welcome’ Theme and Names First Artists
items.summary:
After an inaugural edition last year, the Bukhara Biennial will return to Uzbekistan in 2027, this time with “The Long Welcome” as a theme (after 2025’s theme of “Recipes for Broken Hearts”). As announced this past summer, the artistic director for the next edition—slated to open September 3 and run through November 21—is Kulapat Yantrasast, the revered architect behind museum projects for institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Louvre, Harvard Art Museums, and the Art Institute of Chicago (as well as others while he worked for Tadao Ando).

“At a time when the world needs dialogue and understanding more than ever, culture can bring people together and open space for a shared future,” Bukhara Biennial commissioner Gayane Umerova said in a press release announcing the theme, which will be organized around four parts: Local Hospitality, Co-Creation, Resilience and Biodiversity, and Living Heritage. “For centuries, Bukhara welcomed travelers, craftspeople and merchants from across the world, and that openness shaped its identity. Through the biennial, we want to carry this legacy forward through contemporary art, so that it becomes part of life in the city, creates opportunities for its residents and leaves a lasting cultural legacy.”

Yantrasast added: “The Long Welcome celebrates the spirit of hospitality that made Bukhara worth crossing continents to reach, and worth returning to again and again. When people welcome you into their city, you want to give something back. My hope is that an artist who returns to Bukhara years from now will find that…

items.title: Sir Stanley Wells obituary
items.summary:
Eminent Shakespeare scholar and author who brought together the worlds of academia and the theatre

In 1978 Oxford University Press made Stanley Wells, who has died aged 96, director of a Shakespeare department specially created so that he could produce a new edition of the complete works.

Starting from scratch, he went back to the early printed copies, the quartos and folios, and thought through every editorial and textual decision – how to modernise the spelling and punctuation, and edit stage directions and speakers’ names, while giving the rationales for emendations. The single volume Complete Shakespeare appeared in 1986, edited by Stanley, with Gary Taylor, John Jowett and William Montgomery. It proved to be groundbreaking, startling and controversial.

items.title: The Royal Court’s new mission? To boldly go back to the 60s space race with The Afronauts
items.summary:
Royal Court theatre, London
Ryan Calais Cameron’s ‘true(ish)’ account of a charismatic freedom fighter’s plan to take a Zambian crew to the moon never quite lifts off

Ryan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way.

It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission.

items.title: Simon Brodkin: ‘Which of my pranks went badly wrong? Well, Boris Johnson became PM after the Theresa May one’
items.summary:
The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him

How did you get into comedy?
I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy.

Who did you admire when you were starting out?
It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney.

items.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
items.summary:
Royal & Derngate, Northampton
The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties

Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake.

That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten.

items.title: Nine Night is back and proves itself a modern classic full of secrets, squabbles and laughs
items.summary:
Kiln theatre, London
Exquisitely acted, and directed with lightness and depth, Natasha Gordon’s 2018 tragicomedy about a Jamaican matriarch’s wake is moving and never mawkish

The death of a parent has a way of blowing up the lives of family members it leaves behind. The combustions of grief, greed and secrets revealed around a barely buried coffin litter the tragicomic works of playwrights such as Tracy Letts (August: Osage County) and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins (Appropriate).

You might want to add Natasha Gordon’s debut play to that canon, although it comes wrapped in its own distinct cultural tradition. Its structure revolves around the Caribbean funeral ritual that commemorates the death of a loved one over nine nights. A debut play written by a young Black British woman, featuring an almost entirely Black British cast, it got a huge reaction at the National Theatre in 2018.

items.title: Lend them your ears! Julius Caesar is staged with just four actors – and a great big gong
items.summary:
Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, London
This truncated, candlelit version makes use of skilful percussion to occasionally fill in for oration but loses some of the play’s beauty and power

Any modern reformulation of Julius Caesar may inevitably be compared with Phyllida Lloyd’s innovative, all-female 2012 production, now revived by the Royal Shakespeare Company, which reimagined the tragedy as a play-within-a-play in a women’s prison.

This reworked version, adapted and directed by Joe Hill-Gibbins, does not match its depth and originality but certainly does something different. It is performed at 90 minutes straight-through with just four actors who take on the central roles of conspirators Cassius (Natey Jones) and Brutus (Caoilfhionn Dunne) alongside Mark Antony (Adam Gillen) and Caesar (Kate Duchêne, who also plays the soothsayer and Octavius). It is not as gimmicky as you may think.
